newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil '97 stock gains likely to slow - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil '97 stock gains likely to slow - analysts.

text.p: Brazilian shares, which have soared an unexpectedly strong 30 percent so far this year, are likely to rise at a slower rate in coming months, analysts said.
"The market's return in three months was what we had expected for the whole year. Now it has less room to rise," said Alvaro Maia, head of equity sales at Caspian Securities in Brazil.

Most analysts now think that the rise in the Sao Paulo stock market's Bovespa index will be about 50 or 55 percent for the calendar year -- meaning the bulk of the share increase has already taken place.

Stocks skyrocketed in the first quarter on investor optimism over advances in Brazilian privatizations and legislative votes paving the way to allow Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for a second term.
Caspian's Maia said some shares, particularly in the electrical sector, have already risen sharply and now have limited potential upside.
Power shares had been climbing since early last year on positive prospects for the privatization of federal Eletrobras, CPFL and Eletropaulo -- which are publicly traded.
Some market analysts note two other factors could contribute to slow the bolsa's rally -- a possible hike in U.S. interest rates and Brazil's deteriorating trade balance.
Fears of higher U.S. rates have prompted investors to take profits in the last two sessions as the March 25 meeting of the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee (FOMC) approaches.
Even if there is no U.S. interest rate change in March, many U.S. economists think the increase could come in May.
One immediate impact of a rate hike might be to redirect foreign capital flows back to the United States, where fixed-income assets would be more attractive, analysts said.

Foreign buys were behind much of this year's rally. Net capital inflows to Brazilian bourses under Annex Four rules totalled $1.698 billion in January and February, almost half of last year's total net foreign inflows of $3.593 billion.

Another factor that might cause investors to re-evaluate their positions in Brazilian stocks is the nation's widening trade deficit. In the first two months of 1997, Brazil has rolled up a trade deficit of $2.031 billion -- a sum nearly half that the entire 1996 calendar year trade deficit of $5.539 billion.
Still, Brazil's external accounts appear to be causing more concern among local players than foreigners, according to Sergio Goldman, head of Research at Banco Santander's Brazilian unit.
The stock market's biggest bright spot, analysts said, are of telecommunications stock, and in particular Telebras, and they are likley to bolster the market's upward trend.
"Telebras is the only blue-chip which has not yet been fairly priced," said the head of research at an investment bank, who asked not to be named.
Currently, Telebras preferred trades at around $104 and is projected to reach between $120 and $150 by year's end.

Telebras, which accounts for an average 70 percent of the Sao Paulo bourse's trade, is seen posting higher earnings this year as it will benefit from a new rate adjustment which traders speculate will be announced soon.

In 1996, Telebras' net consolidated profit soared to 2.756 billion reais. The gain reflected an increase in traffic, a reduction in costs and increased earnings due to tariff restructuring that took effect in November 1995.
And some believe privatization prospects for the telecommunications sector have not yet been fully factored in.

The Communications Ministry will kick off the privatization of the telecom industry by offering private investors concessions to operate Band B cellular services. The government will be taking bids early next month.
Also this year, it plans to begin selling off some of Telebras' subsidiaries, probably Sao Paulo state telecom Telesp and long-distance unit Embratel.
((-- Sao Paulo Newsroom 5511 2485412))
